paper_topic: DelexGate-ASA: schema canonicalization for activation steering under tool-schema churn (negative result)
anchor_paper: ASA / Activation Steering Adapter (Wang et al., 2026)

nodes.text: Tool-calling has become a critical capability for large language model (LLM) agents, enabling them to interact with external APIs and execute real-world actions (Patil et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023).
nodes.display_label: tool-calling is critical for LLM agents

nodes.text: In production deployments, however, tool schemas evolve over time due to API versioning, refactoring, or style changes—a phenomenon we term schema churn.
This poses a challenge for methods that rely on schema-specific calibration, as their learned representations may not transfer when identifiers change.
ASA (Activation Steering Adapter) (Wang et al., 2026) is a promising training-free method that improves tool-calling by manipulating model activations at inference time.
ASA learns a steering vector and linear probe from labeled examples to control whether the model enters tool mode.
However, since these assets are computed from hidden states that encode schema identifiers, they may be sensitive to lexical churn.

We hypothesize that canonicalizing schemas to a stable placeholder vocabulary (e.g., replacing get weather(location, unit) with tool 0(arg 0 0, arg 0 1)) before ASA processing could make the representation space invariant to surface-level identifier changes.
nodes.display_label: hypothesis: canonicalize to placeholders for invariance

nodes.text: We propose DelexGate-ASA, which applies this canonicalization strategy: schemas are transformed to generic identifiers before ASA calibration and inference, with outputs remapped back to real identifiers.
On the BFCL v3 benchmark (Patil et al., 2025), DelexGate-ASA degrades clean-schema AST accuracy by 15.2 percentage points (from 0.768 to 0.616) while providing no robustness benefit under churn.
nodes.display_label: AST accuracy drops 15.2 pts on BFCL v3

nodes.text: The failure reveals that LLMs rely on semantic information in parameter names for correct argument-value mapping—canonicalization removes these essential cues.
First, we document a well-motivated approach (schema canonicalization for activation steering) that fails, saving future researchers from pursuing similar directions.
Second, we reveal that semantic information in parameter names is essential for function-call accuracy—LLMs cannot reliably map values to generic placeholders even when descriptions are preserved.

Third, we show that ASA’s learned assets are inherently robust to lexical churn: recalibration provides no benefit over simple reuse, indicating that degradation under churn stems from base model sensitivity rather than ASA asset drift.
nodes.display_label: C3: ASA assets robust; base model sensitive

N8 forks via evidence into the result chain. The renderer should detect N6 as a heavy join.
